opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the guiding principle, for me, is that you can't just ask a model to "generate a lot of diverse data" and expect diversity to come out. If you do that naively, you get mode collapse. The model keeps returning to its favorite, most probable outputs, and you end up with thousands of examples that are slight paraphrases of each other. Scale alone doesn't buy you coverage.

So the idea of doing it in stages is really about decomposing the space before you fill it in. First you think about the structure of what you want to cover. That might be topics, or types of reasoning, or situations, or personas, or levels of difficulty. You enumerate or sample along those axes deliberately. Only then do you generate the actual content, conditioned on those specific seeds. Each stage constrains the next, so diversity is something you engineer at the top of the pipeline rather than hope for at the bottom.

There's a second piece that matters just as much, which is filtering and critique between stages. Generation is cheap, but quality and diversity both degrade if you don't prune. So you generate, you verify, you deduplicate, and you check whether you're over-representing some region. Then you go back and push into the areas that are thin. It's almost like an iterative search over the data distribution, not a single sampling pass.

And underneath all of that is a philosophical point I care about. Smaller models, or models trained on carefully constructed data, can do surprisingly well, sometimes better than models trained on much more raw data. That's because what matters isn't just quantity. It's the shape of the distribution you're teaching. If you're thoughtful about that shape, staging, conditioning, filtering, you can distill really useful knowledge and capabilities without needing everything to come from brute-force scale.

r001.rationale: The response advocates structured, staged generation and filtering instead of naive bulk generation, but it does not state that synthetic training data should be qualitatively different from easily generated internet-like data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the guiding principle, I'd say, is that diversity doesn't come for free from a model. If you just prompt a large language model and say "give me a hundred examples of X," you'll get a hundred examples that look suspiciously alike. The model has its own distribution, its own favorite phrasings, its own favorite topics, and it collapses toward the mode very quickly. So the whole motivation for staging the generation is to fight that collapse deliberately rather than hoping it won't happen.

The way I think about it is that you want to decouple the decision about what to generate from the act of generating it. In the first stage, you're not writing data at all. You're generating the space of things the data should cover: the topics, the scenarios, the entities, the constraints, whatever the relevant axes of variation are for your task. And crucially, that stage is where you can inspect and intervene. You can look at the distribution of seeds, notice that eighty percent of them are about cooking and travel, and fix it before you've spent any compute on the actual examples. If you let the model do everything in one shot, that structure is buried inside the outputs and you only discover the skew after the fact, if ever.

Then in the later stages, you condition on those seeds. Each example is grounded in something specific, so the model has a reason to go somewhere different each time instead of drifting back to its default. We saw this very clearly in some of our earlier work on symbolic knowledge distillation and in the commonsense generation line of research. When you give the model a concrete anchor, a particular event or a particular person in a particular situation, it produces knowledge that is much more varied and much less generic than when you just ask it open-endedly.

There's also a quality dimension that comes along with this. Once generation is staged, you can put filtering or verification between stages, so you're not just diversifying but also pruning the junk before it propagates. A critic model, a classifier, even simple heuristics. That matters because diversity and quality tend to pull against each other. If you sample aggressively for variety you get more noise, and if you filter hard for quality you tend to keep the boring, safe examples. Staging gives you a place to manage that tension explicitly.

And the deeper point, I think, is that the student model learns the distribution you show it. If the synthetic data is narrow, the student will be narrow, and it will be confidently narrow, which is worse. So the real principle is: treat diversity as something you design and measure at each stage, not something you hope emerges at the end.

r001.rationale: The response says staged generation should counter the model’s repetitive default distribution, but it does not state that synthetic training data should be qualitatively different from easily generated internet-like data.

astra-6.text: The guiding principle is that you want to diversify the underlying ideas, not just the wording. If you simply ask a model to generate a lot of examples, it can keep returning to the same familiar patterns. So you break the process into stages: first explore a broad range of topics or situations, then generate examples within those, and then check their quality. That gives you opportunities to steer toward areas that are underrepresented. The goal is to get broader coverage of the space, rather than just more data.

r001.rationale: The response advocates diversifying ideas and avoiding repetitive familiar patterns, but it does not state that synthetic training data should be qualitatively different from easily generated internet-like data.

sol-6.1.text: The guiding principle is that you don’t want to generate more and more of essentially the same thing. If you simply ask a model to produce examples repeatedly, it can gravitate toward a fairly narrow set of patterns. So you break the process into stages: first explore a broad range of situations or concepts, and then generate examples within those different contexts. That gives you more control over coverage and diversity. At each stage, you want to check both quality and whether you’re actually adding something new, rather than just increasing the volume of data.

r001.rationale: The response calls for broader coverage and novel examples, but does not state that synthetic training data should be qualitatively different from easily generated internet-like data.
